title: House of Sand and Fog
full_review:
An unopened letter becomes the catalyst for tragedy in the grim drama "House of Sand and Fog" (Dreamworks).

Dreamworks is hoping against hope that "House" will elevate its depressed box office to end a bad year on a good note. But unfortunately for the company, this is not the type of movie that is likely to have mass appeal. Debut director Vadim Perelman's tragic tale reveals with searing emotion the consequences actions -- both good and bad -- can have on frail human beings. It is moving and poignant, with a brilliant performance by Ben Kingsley. While the film's crushing sadness overwhelms the viewer, leaving one drained, the film's flaws cannot be dismissed.

Massoud Amir Behrani (Kingsley) is an immigrant and former colonel in the shah of Iran's air force who has been struggling for years to maintain the facade of prosperity. He lives with his wife, Nadi (Shohreh Aghdashloo), and teenage son, Esmail (Jonathan Ahdout), in a lavish apartment in a tony California neighborhood they can barely afford. Behrani cleans highways by day and sits behind the counter of a tiny gas station market by night, yet everyone believes he has a high-powered job with Boeing.

But now he has finally found an opportunity to advance: a Northern California bungalow by the sea put on the auction block at a fraction of its real worth. He snaps up the property with the hopes of reselling it at a big profit. This is not profiteering, but a means to survive and restore his family to the comfort they once enjoyed.

The house Behrani acquires is the one Kathy Nicolo (Jennifer Connelly) had been left by her father. Kathy, a recovering addict whose husband split eight months ago, was evicted from the house when she failed to pay business taxes. The whole affair, however, turns out to be a computer glitch, as Kathy never owed the $500 the county claimed. But Kathy also never bothered to open her mail and missed all the warnings.

Completely at loose ends, sleeping in her car and washing up in public restrooms, Kathy is helped by the kindness of a stranger: Deputy Sheriff Lester Burdon (Ron Eldard). Married (but unhappily, of course) with two children, Lester's kind gestures ignite passion and he and Kathy begin an affair, whereby he abruptly ends his marriage.

The rest of the film unfolds with the characters involved in an intricate string of missteps, accusations and poor judgments. The film succeeds in keeping the viewers off-balance by not allowing them to choose sides. Behrani now owns title to the house free and clear. His reasons for acquiring it are justifiable. But Kathy has been wronged by the county, so her feelings of outrage are understandable, despite her own part in losing the house. The film also deftly builds tension as tempers rise and desperation's cold grip takes hold, pushing the characters toward reckless and devastating deeds.

However, throughout the film, nagging inconsistencies pop up. Kathy and Lester's relationship moves fast, and while the speed is not unbelievable, the lack of spark between these two actors makes it hard to be convinced that they have "found" each other, as Lester puts it. Contrarily, the last third of the film slows considerably, until it suddenly puts things in motion toward its bleak ending.

Kingsley is fascinating to watch. He literally disappears into his character, a difficult thing to accomplish considering his distinctive looks. Precisely buttoning his crisp white shirt, he can only be one person: someone who, through no misdeed of his own, has fallen from his lofty footing and now must toil to regain it in a foreign country while watching spoiled Americans take their advantages for granted.

Unfortunately, praise cannot be lavished on Connelly. Tears flow easily from her intense eyes. But crying and looking bleary-eyed are not the same as conveying true heart-ripping emotion. She plays Kathy (who is casually wooed into drinking by Lester after three years of sobriety) as distant and wounded, but fails to make a connection with her lover and the audience.

Eldard is the real weak link. His performance is unconvincing, a problem that may be due in part to his underwritten character. He's also an unlikable bully who seems to have been just waiting for the chance to abandon his family.

"House of Sand and Fog" is the story of the American dream gone wrong. It doesn't condescend to celebrate the dire choices its characters take. Instead, it shows the horrific consequences both action and inaction can sometimes create.

Because of some sexual encounters with shadowy nudity, an extramarital affair, brief but intense violence and intermittent rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
